article.title: Girl Child
article.author: Elahe Amani
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. October 11, the International Day of the Girl Child, arrived amid a period of unprecedented turmoil and shifting political realities. From war and violence in Iran and Yemen to political unrest and violent protests across parts of Europe, including Albania and France, a climate of instability continues to threaten human rights, peace, and security. Across many parts of the world, the rise of religious extremism, authoritarian governance, and right-wing populist movements has intensified resistance to gender equality and undermined efforts to protect the rights, dignity, and safety of girls. Invoking tradition, religious authority, parental rights, and the preservation of the “natural family,” some of these movements seek to restrict women’s autonomy and weaken the institutions designed to protect women and girls. The recognition of the “girl child” as a distinct focus of international advocacy marked an important milestone in the global struggle for gender equality. At the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995, The Girl Child was established as one of the 12 critical areas of concern in the Beijing Platform for Action. This recognition affirmed an essential principle: discrimination against women often begins in childhood, and addressing gender inequality requires specific attention to the rights, needs, and experiences of girls. The Beijing Platform addressed discrimination in education, health and nutrition, child labor, violence, harmful practices, and girls’ participation in social, economic, and political life. It helped institutionalize the girl child as a central category in international women’s rights advocacy, connecting the inequalities girls experience in childhood with the broader structures of gender discrimination that shape their lives. In subsequent years, UN General Assembly resolutions continued to address the rights of the girl child, while international agencies expanded their focus on girls’ education, child marriage, violence, exploitation, and adolescent health. In 2011, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 66/170, designating October 11 as the International Day of the Girl Child. The annual observance created an international platform to advance girls’ rights, amplify their voices, and recognize their leadership. Related: Iran’s Employment Crisis Is Driving Women Out of the Workforce The terminology itself also deserves reflection. The term “girl child” served an important political purpose: it made girls visible in policy discussions where the broader categories of “women” and “children” could obscure their distinct experiences of discrimination. Yet the history of this terminology is not without criticism. Historian Sarah Bellows-Blakely, in her work on the history of girl-focused development, examines how international development institutions have sometimes portrayed girls in the Global South primarily as vulnerable victims in need of intervention, rather than as individuals with agency, political voices, and diverse lived experiences. This critical perspective invites us to ask an important question: Who defines girls’ needs, whose knowledge shapes international policy, and how can girls themselves become active participants in decisions affecting their lives? Why does the girl child deserve our urgent attention today? Because recognition alone is not enough. The rights of girls remain threatened by the intersecting realities of poverty, armed conflict, forced displacement, disability, discrimination, and humanitarian crises. For girls living at the intersection of these vulnerabilities, the consequences can be especially severe. Consider the scale of the challenges facing children worldwide. More than 520 million children, over one in five globally, live within 50 kilometers of violent conflict events, according to research published by the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). Approximately 1.6 billion children live in countries affected by conflict. These figures reflect different levels of exposure: proximity to violent events does not mean that every child experiences violence directly, but it highlights the enormous number of children growing up amid insecurity and instability. In conflict-affected communities, the destruction of schools ( the air strike on Feb 28, 2026 on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab 120 children killed ), loss of livelihoods, displacement, and breakdown of protective institutions can further heighten these risks. Discriminatory laws, harmful practices, and inadequate enforcement of children’s rights may allow these conditions to persist. Girls who are already marginalized because of poverty, ethnicity, disability, displacement, or other forms of discrimination may face multiple and overlapping barriers to protection. Related: Mother’s Day 2026: Reclaiming Motherhood as a Call for Peace, Justice, and Collective Care Poverty presents another profound challenge. According to UNICEF, approximately 412 million children lived in extreme monetary poverty in 2024, while an estimated 417 million children in low- and middle-income countries experienced severe deprivation in at least two essential areas of life, including education, health, nutrition, housing, sanitation, and water. These figures include both girls and boys and illustrate the magnitude of childhood deprivation, while underscoring the need for more comprehensive, gender-disaggregated data. Poverty, conflict, displacement, and discrimination do not operate in isolation. They intersect and reinforce one another, creating conditions that place girls at heightened risk of exploitation, violence, and child marriage. When families face economic hardship, armed conflict, or displacement, girls may be forced to leave school, lose access to health care and other essential services, or face decisions that prioritize immediate survival over their rights, well-being, and future. In some circumstances, child marriage is used as a misguided coping mechanism to reduce a family’s perceived financial burden, respond to insecurity, or conform to entrenched social and cultural expectations. The consequences of child marriage can extend throughout a girl’s life: interrupted education, early pregnancy, serious health risks, exposure to domestic and sexual violence, diminished economic opportunities, and restricted participation in decisions affecting her own future. The loss is not only individual. Families, communities, and societies are also deprived of girls’ talents, knowledge, creativity, and leadership. Child marriage, therefore, must not be understood simply as an isolated cultural practice or an individual family decision. It must also be examined within the broader social, economic, political, and institutional structures that constrain girls’ choices, perpetuate gender inequality, and undermine their fundamental rights. Globally, the legal landscape remains deeply concerning. According to UNESCO’s HerAtlas data, only 26% of countries set 18 as the minimum legal age of marriage without exceptions. In approximately 54% of countries, exceptions permit marriage before the age of 18, while in 18% of countries, laws still allow marriage below 18. These figures illustrate the gap between recognizing 18 as the appropriate minimum age and establishing an absolute legal prohibition on child marriage. The WORLD Policy Analysis Center’s legal database identifies numerous countries and jurisdictions where laws may permit girls to marry before the age of 18 under certain circumstances. These include Bahrain, Djibouti, the Federated States of Micronesia, Iran, Kuwait, Lebanon, Mali, Mauritania, North Korea, Pakistan, Qatar, Sudan, Timor-Leste, and Yemen. The United Kingdom also requires a jurisdiction-specific distinction: Scotland and Northern Ireland permit marriage at 16 under applicable legal conditions. The database additionally identifies Bangladesh, Botswana, Brunei, and the United Arab Emirates as having religious or customary law exceptions that may permit marriage below 18. These classifications should be checked against current national and subnational legislation, as laws and exceptions change over time. Particularly alarming is the evidence emerging from Iran, where technology is being used in ways that may facilitate and normalize child marriage. The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) published an investigative report titled Child Marriage in the Digital Age , examining the Iranian government licensed matchmaking platform Adam va Hava (“Adam and Eve”) and its role in facilitating the marriage of minors. According to HRANA’s investigation, although the platform’s terms reportedly state that female users must be older than 15, its registration system accepts birth years corresponding to children as young as 12. Search filters reportedly allow users to browse prospective spouses from age 13, making profiles of minors accessible. These findings raise serious concerns about the protection of children online and the normalization of marriage involving girls who have not reached adulthood. The investigation also examines the platform’s institutional connections. HRANA traces its ownership to the Imam Reza Society, led by Hossein Yekta, a senior figure associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Yekta has been subject to European Union sanctions related to human rights violations. The platform has also reportedly received promotion through Iranian state media. HRANA situates its operation within a broader government-backed matchmaking system that expanded following the 2021 Youth Population Law, which encouraged the development of authorized matchmaking platforms. These developments must be considered alongside Iran’s Civil Code, which generally sets the minimum marriage age at 13 lunar years for girls and 15 lunar years for boys, while allowing marriage below those ages with the consent of a legal guardian and judicial approval. This framework falls far short of establishing 18 as an absolute minimum age for marriage and raises serious concerns about Iran’s compliance with international child-protection standards, including the principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The response from international civil society has been significant. HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations issued a joint appeal urging major technology companies to take action. They called on Google and Meta to remove the application from the Google Play Store and on Meta to address promotional accounts on Instagram and Threads. According to the appeal, an Instagram account with approximately 192,000 followers had been used to promote the platform and its matchmaking services, including content involving minors. The organizations also called for greater transparency regarding ownership, safeguarding measures, and the enforcement of child-protection policies. Related: Disconnected in War While after the joint appeal of HRANA and 23 other human rights organizations Google removed the "Adam and Eve" app from Google Play on October 9, 2026, for policy violations and Meta investigated the findings and removed related promotional and external entities from its platforms (including Instagram and Threads). However, this case raises a fundamental question: What responsibility do governments, technology companies, and international institutions have when digital platforms facilitate practices that place children’s rights and safety at risk? Technology should expand opportunities, access to information, and human connection, not provide new mechanisms for exposing children to exploitation or normalizing practices that compromise their autonomy and well-being. Child marriage is not simply a matter of tradition or private choice. When discriminatory laws permit it, institutions facilitate it, and digital platforms make it more visible and accessible, the issue becomes one of public accountability and the protection of fundamental human rights. Every girl has the right to childhood, education, bodily autonomy, safety, and the opportunity to determine her own future. Ensuring those rights requires unequivocal legal protections, effective enforcement, responsible technology governance, and sustained international action to eliminate marriage before the age of 18, without exceptions. The reality is that child marriage risks to girls' safety, physical integrity, health, and autonomy. In an extensive research on Child marriage and intimate partner violence: A global meta-analysis with the title of “ Prevalence of intimate partner violence among child marriage victims and the comparison with adult marriages: a systematic review and meta-analysis” 38 studies involving approximately 395,000 women married as children across five continents were reviewed and the findings are “ it is estimated that 35% had experienced intimate partner violence during their lifetime and 24% in the previous 12 months. Compared with women who married as adults, women married as children had 42% higher odds of experiencing intimate partner violence over their lifetime and 37% higher odds in the preceding year. Other research such as Honor-based violence against children: A systematic review with the title of “ Honor, violence, and children: A systematic scoping review of global evidence (2024) in the Journal Child Abuse & Neglect. This research identifies recurring harms including violence, family rejection and control, homicide, and forced or early marriage. The research highlights the risks of family violence and homicide, though it does not establish that child marriage itself causes honor killings. Child marriage in Iran and other countries where it is legally permitted requires a holistic examination of power dynamics, gender-based norms, and the ways violence is portrayed in the media and normalized in the public consciousness. The issue is not merely the occurrence of a crime, but also how such acts are represented sometimes in ways that normalize or even legitimize them. A crucial question is whether Iranian media is challenging these deeply rooted gender norms and defending women’s and girls’ fundamental rights to life, safety, and autonomy or, instead, reinforcing the very structures that undermine them. Combating so-called honor killings of the girl childs cannot be achieved simply by condemning perpetrators after the fact. It requires confronting the gender-based power structures that place girls in vulnerable situations, questioning the social and cultural norms that enable such violence, and ensuring that legal and institutional protections prevent child marriage and safeguard girls from harm. The legislative history of Iran’s Protection of Women Against Violence bill reflects the challenges of securing meaningful legal protection. Also referred to as the Protection, Dignity, and Security of Women Against Violence and later renamed the Prevention of Harassment and Promotion of Security for Women Against Misbehavior , the bill was reportedly withdrawn from the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) by President Masoud Pezeshkian’s cabinet in September 2025. For more than 15 years, the proposed legislation has moved back and forth among successive administrations, the judiciary, and Parliament, illustrating the prolonged struggle to establish comprehensive legal protections against violence toward women and girls. Related: March 8 in the Shadow of War: Iranian Women and the Enduring Struggle for Gender Justice Needless to say that child marriage is not only happening in global south. In the United States, as of October 8, 2026, 32 states reportedly still permit marriage before the age of 18 under certain legal conditions, including parental consent, court approval, or other exceptions. The laws vary significantly from state to state. California has recently prohibited marriage for anyone under 18, without exceptions, joining the states that have eliminated child marriage through legislation. The 32 states identified as still allowing marriage before age 18 are Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. Nearly 300,000 children were married in the U.S. between 2000 and 2018. The vast majority were girls wed to adult men. Ending child marriage requires more than prohibiting marriage before the age of 18. It demands enforceable legal protections without exceptions, equal access to quality education, economic and social support for families, protection during humanitarian emergencies, and the meaningful participation of girls in decisions affecting their lives. On protecting the child girl rights, dignity and safety, we must move beyond celebrating girls’ potential and acknowledging their vulnerability. We must confront the structures that deny them safety, dignity, equality, and opportunity. Protecting girls means addressing not only the violations they experience, but also the intersecting inequalities and structural conditions that allow those violations to persist. Every girl deserves the freedom to grow up safely, complete her education, exercise autonomy over her life, and shape her own future. The promise of Beijing remains unfinished. Our responsibility is to turn its commitments into lived realities for every girl, especially those whose voices are too often unheard and whose rights are most at risk.
